--- title: "Piping" description: "Using the pipe operator to have more readable code" author: - Etienne Bacher - Will Gearty date: "2026-11-16" brand: _brand/_brand.yml format: revealjs: output-file: index-slides.html toc: false css: style/template.css slide-number: c/t include-in-header: style/header.html include-after-body: style/footer.html execute: echo: true eval: false warning: false message: false freeze: auto editor: markdown: wrap: 72 --- ## Objectives
Learn how to use the pipe operator (`|>`) to write more readable code. # Without the pipe ## Example
We want to process `mtcars`: - keep the first 10 rows - keep observations where `cyl >= 6` - sort the data by `am` . . .
Two common approaches: intermediate objects or nested calls. ## Intermediate objects
Overwrite the same object at each step: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res <- head(mtcars, 10) res <- subset(res, cyl >= 6) res <- sort_by(res, ~ am) ``` ::: . . .
- Renaming `res` means renaming every occurrence. - If one step fails, we must rerun the whole block. ## Intermediate objects
Use temporary names: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tmp1 <- head(mtcars, 10) tmp2 <- subset(tmp1, cyl >= 6) res <- sort_by(tmp2, ~ am) ``` ::: . . .
- Pollutes the environment with temporary objects. - Adding a step means renaming many objects. ## Nested calls
Run all calls at once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3|2-5|"} res <- sort_by( subset( head(mtcars, 10), cyl >= 6 ), ~ am ) ``` ::: . . .
No intermediate objects, but we must read from the inside out. # Introducing the pipe ## Using `|>`
The pipe passes the output of the left-hand side to the next call: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res <- head(mtcars, 10) |> subset(cyl >= 6) |> sort_by(~ am) ``` ::: . . . Read it as "**and then**": - keep the first 10 rows, *and then* - filter, *and then* - sort. ## Using `|>`
- No intermediate objects. - Operations are read in the order they run. . . .
`|>` is available since R 4.1 (2021). ## Assigning the output
We can also assign at the end of the chain with `->`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(mtcars, 10) |> subset(cyl >= 6) |> sort_by(~ am) -> res ``` ::: # Using `_` ## Piping to non-first arguments
`grepl()` takes the vector to check in **second** position: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} let <- letters[1:6] grepl("a|e", let) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: . . . Piping without care gives incorrect code: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} let |> grepl("a|e") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in grepl(let, "a|e"): argument 'pattern' has length > 1 and only the first element will be used ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ## The placeholder `_`
`_` tells the piped data where to go: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} let |> grepl("a|e", x = _) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: . . .
It also works for extraction: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mtcars |> _$drat |> mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.596563 ``` ::: ::: ## Restrictions of `_` Available since R 4.2 (2022). . . .
Must be used with a named argument: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} let |> grepl("a|e", _) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in grepl("a|e", "_"): pipe placeholder can only be used as a named argument (:1:8) ``` ::: ::: . . .
Only one `_` per function call: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mtcars$drat |> cor(x = _, y = _) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in cor(x = "_", y = "_"): pipe placeholder may only appear once (:1:16) ``` ::: ::: # Anonymous functions ## Named functions
Named functions are defined first and can be used multiple times:
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_function <- function(x) { (x - mean(x)) / sd(x) } lapply(my_list, my_function) my_function(1:3) ``` ::: ## Anonymous functions
Anonymous functions are created on the fly and can only be used once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lapply(my_list, function(x) { (x - mean(x)) / sd(x) }) ``` ::: . . .
In a pipe, wrap it in parentheses and call it with `()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mtcars |> subset(cyl == 4) |> (function(d) lm(mpg ~ disp, data = d))() ``` ::: # What about `%>%`? ## `%>%` vs `|>`
- `%>%` comes from the `magrittr` package. - It was widely used in the `tidyverse`. - It inspired `|>` in base R. . . .
For simple cases, both behave the same. . . .
We recommend `|>` since it is always available, and doesn't require an extra package.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
